summaries.example: Imagine a doctor gives medicine to a very sick patient to ease severe pain. The doctor does not want to cause harm, but worries about a bad result. The doctrine asks whether the good goal, the way the medicine works, the doctor’s purpose, and the size of the risk make the action acceptable. It also asks whether a safer choice was available.
summaries.summary: The Doctrine of Double Effect is a way of thinking about hard moral choices. An action may lead to a good result and a bad result at the same time. The doctrine says the bad result can sometimes be allowed when it is not the person’s goal, is not used as the way to get the good result, and there is a strong enough reason for accepting it. The person should also try to limit the harm and consider other choices. The entry explains examples involving self-defense, medical care, war, rescue, and runaway trolleys. It also warns that expecting harm does not automatically make an action right. Critics question whether people describe harms as “side effects” partly because they already approve of the action, and whether one rule really explains every example.
key_ideas: The doctrine separates what someone means to do from what they expect may happen.
It says a bad result might sometimes be allowed as a side effect, but not simply because it was expected.
The action should be good or at least not wrong by itself.
The good result must not be achieved by using the bad result as a tool.
People should avoid or reduce harm and look for less harmful choices.
Philosophers disagree about whether one rule can explain all these cases.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea helps people discuss difficult choices without looking only at the final result. It draws attention to purpose, methods, risks, and the duty to reduce harm. It is used in debates about medical treatment, rescue, warfare, and machines that must respond to danger. The entry also shows why careful thinking is needed: a good goal alone does not excuse every harmful action.

important_terms.definition: A moral idea about actions that bring about both a good result and a bad result.
The result a person is trying to bring about on purpose.
A result a person expects might happen but is not trying to make happen.
A bad result that happens alongside a good goal, rather than being used to achieve it.
A good result must be important enough to justify allowing the bad result.

questions_to_think_about: Does it matter whether someone wanted a bad result or only expected it?
How should we compare a serious harm with a very important benefit?
When should a person choose a safer but less helpful option?
Can two actions with the same results still be morally different?

summaries.example: Suppose a runaway trolley is heading toward five people. A bystander can pull a switch so that it reaches a different track with one person. Many people judge switching differently from pushing a person in front of the trolley to stop it. One explanation is that, when switching, the death of the one is foreseen but not used as the means of saving the five; when pushing, the person’s body is used as part of the plan. The entry stresses that this explanation is disputed and does not by itself settle the case.
summaries.summary: The Doctrine of Double Effect holds that, in some circumstances, an agent may permissibly bring about a serious harm as an unintended but anticipated consequence of pursuing a good end, even though bringing about that harm as a means to the same end would be impermissible. Standard versions add several conditions: the act itself must be acceptable or neutral, the good effect must be intended, the bad effect must not produce the good effect, and the benefit must be proportionate to the harm. The source also suggests that responsible agents should seek less harmful alternatives and reduce foreseeable damage. Applications include the contrast between terror and tactical bombing, some medical decisions, self-defense, rescue, and trolley cases. However, the entry emphasizes that double effect is not a complete permission: proportionality, duties, conventions, patient preferences, and other substantive judgments matter. Critics raise the problem of closeness, question whether intention descriptions are morally neutral, and propose accounts based on direct and indirect agency. The entry concludes that the varied cases may not all be explained by one unified principle.
key_ideas: Traditional formulations distinguish intending grave harm as a means from permitting it as an unintended consequence of pursuing a good end.

A plausible version requires an action to be morally acceptable or neutral in itself, the good rather than the bad effect to be intended, no use of the bad effect as the means, and a proportionately serious reason.
Foreseeing harm is not enough to justify it. Agents may need to minimize harm, consider alternatives, and accept some cost or risk to reduce it.
The distinction between intended and foreseen consequences is not the same as the distinction between doing harm and allowing harm.
Critics argue that judgments about whether an effect was intended may be influenced by prior moral approval or disapproval, a pattern called the Side Effect Effect.
The entry questions whether cases such as risky rescue, self-sacrifice, medical treatment, warfare, and trolley choices are best explained by one principle.
summaries.why_it_matters: The doctrine influences reasoning about medicine, war, rescue, self-defense, and emerging technologies. Its importance lies not only in its possible conclusions but also in the questions it forces us to ask: What is the agent trying to do? Is the harm part of the method? Could the harm be reduced? Is the benefit sufficient? The entry’s criticisms caution against treating intention as a simple loophole or using a general formula instead of examining the concrete moral and institutional rules governing a case.

important_terms.definition: A moral principle concerning cases in which an action produces both a beneficial outcome and a serious harmful outcome.
The outcome or feature of an action that an agent chooses as part of the plan.
An outcome the agent anticipates without choosing it as the aim or as a step toward that aim.
A harmful outcome that accompanies an action aimed at a good result but is not the route by which that result is produced.
The requirement that the benefit be weighty enough to justify permitting the harm, considering relevant circumstances.
Agency in which a person is deliberately involved in a plan so that this involvement helps achieve the agent’s purpose, contrasted with harmful indirect agency.
The view that permissibility depends only on outcomes, or on outcomes that are foreseen, rather than on intentions or motives.
The difficulty of drawing a principled line between a harm that is a side effect and one that is sufficiently connected to the plan to count as a means.

questions_to_think_about: Can the same harmful outcome be a side effect in one case but a means in another? What would make the difference principled?
Does proportionality merely restate that there must be a good enough reason, or does it provide useful moral guidance?
If an agent intentionally imposes a lower risk of death to prevent a greater risk, is that harm a means rather than a side effect?
Could people’s moral judgments influence how they describe an outcome as intended or unintended?
Should an ethical rule for trolley cases be used as a model for programming autonomous vehicles?

summaries.example: A town’s emergency team must rescue people from a dangerous building. One plan has a small chance of hurting a person while giving that person a much better chance of survival than staying inside. The team does not want the injury, but it knows the risk is present. Double-effect reasoning asks whether the rescue itself is aimed at saving the person, whether the injury is being used as a tool, whether the team has a strong enough reason, and whether a safer plan exists. The source notes that such risky rescues may challenge a simple version of the doctrine, because choosing the rescue may involve deliberately imposing a lower risk to avoid a greater one.
summaries.summary: The Doctrine of Double Effect is a framework for thinking about actions that produce both good and bad results. It says that a serious harm may sometimes be permissible when the harm is foreseen but not intended, the action is itself acceptable, the good result does not come through the harm, and the reason for accepting the harm is strong enough. The agent should also reduce the harm and consider safer alternatives. The entry applies this idea to cases such as tactical bombing, medical care, self-defense, heroic rescue, and trolley problems. It also explains why the principle is controversial. Foreseeing harm does not by itself justify it, and intention is not the same as merely causing or allowing something. Critics question whether the difference between means and side effects is always clear, whether people describe outcomes differently depending on their moral judgment, and whether risky rescues and other examples involve direct agency. The source leaves open whether a single principle can explain all these cases.
key_ideas: Double-effect reasoning treats intention as morally important, but it does not say that every unintended harm is acceptable.
The harmful result must not be the means by which the good result is achieved.
A strong enough reason, attention to alternatives, and efforts to limit harm are central to serious versions of the principle.
The same distinction appears in cases about bombing, pain treatment, self-defense, rescue, and trolley switches, but the cases may involve different moral issues.
Some critics say the line between an intended means and a foreseen side effect can be unclear, especially when the harm is very closely connected to the action.
The entry examines whether moral approval affects how people label an outcome as intended or accidental.
summaries.why_it_matters: The doctrine gives people a vocabulary for discussing difficult decisions. It encourages them to examine purpose, method, expected consequences, proportionality, and alternatives rather than relying on a simple rule such as “the result was good.” It also shows why moral decisions in healthcare, warfare, rescue, and technology require attention to context and to other duties, not just one formula.

important_terms.definition: A principle used to judge actions that have both a helpful result and a harmful result.
What an actor chooses as the purpose of an action or as a step in carrying it out.
What an actor predicts will happen, even though the actor does not choose it as the purpose.
A harmful result that is expected but is not the goal or the method for reaching the goal.
A test asking whether the good result is important enough to permit the bad result.
A difference between harming someone as part of a plan and harming someone who is affected without being used in that plan.
A philosophical view that says the moral importance of an action depends only on its results or expected results.

questions_to_think_about: Why might someone judge switching a trolley differently from pushing a person to stop it?
Is knowing that harm will happen morally different from choosing harm as part of a plan?
What should count as a proportionate reason for accepting serious harm?
Can a rescue be justified if it deliberately lowers a person’s risk but still exposes that person to danger?
Does one principle explain all the examples, or do medical, military, and rescue cases need separate rules?
